newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk MP commission okays secularist schooling bill.
newsitem.headline: Turk MP commission okays secularist schooling bill.

text.p: A Turkish parliamentary commission on Tuesday approved a secularist education bill bitterly opposed by the country's powerful Islamists, parliament officials said.
They said a general assembly debate and vote on the draft law was likely to be held on Wednesday after nine days of rowdy discussions in the planning and budget commission.
Islamists, who have taken to the streets to protest against the bill, see the reforms as a threat to religious education.
Under the draft law, compulsory state schooling will be extended to eight years from five, effectively bringing an end to the primary section of Islamic schools, known as Imam Hatips.
The education plan was a key element of military demands for a crackdown on rising religious activism under the Islamist-led government of former prime minister Necmettin Erbakan.
The secularist pressure helped edge Erbakan out of office in June and led to the appointment of a right-left government under Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz.
The commission has given its approval to plans for consumers to contribute to the school reforms, forecast to cost 1,000 trillion lira ($613 million) over the next three years.

Under the plans, a 10 percent levy is to be imposed on tobacco and alcoholic drinks. Contributions will also come from car registrations, horse racing and football pools gambling, as well as weapons and hunting licences.

Airline tickets, television advertising fees and mobile phone subscriptions, along with tax and custom declarations will also be subject to the funding plans. Some bourse transactions will also contribute to the education reforms.
